title: Why Quantum Mechanics: The Experiments
intro: Three experiments, Stern–Gerlach magnets, three polarisers and a single particle in an interferometer, that no classical picture can explain, worked through with numbers. Each one forces a rule of quantum mechanics: amplitudes that add and cancel, probabilities that are squares, and measurements that change what they measure.

blocks.text: What you need first
Nothing beyond school algebra and the idea of a probability as a number between 0 and 1. This is the first page of the shelf; it uses no quantum mechanics, only what was seen in the laboratory.
What you will be able to do

items: Describe the Stern–Gerlach, three-polariser and interferometer experiments and predict their counts with the simple rules given here.
Explain which everyday (classical) assumption each experiment breaks.
Tell apart adding probabilities and adding amplitudes, and compute both for the same experiment.
List what any theory of these experiments has to supply, which the rest of the shelf then builds.

blocks.text: Why start with experiments

Quantum mechanics has a reputation for being strange, and the strangeness is not an invention of theorists. It was forced on physicists between about 1900 and 1930 by experiments that gave answers no classical picture could give. If you learn the mathematics first, it looks like a set of arbitrary rules: states are complex vectors, probabilities are squares, measurements change things. If you see the experiments first, each rule becomes the obvious answer to a question the laboratory asked.

This page walks through three experiments in their modern, cleaned-up form. They are chosen because each is simple enough to work out with pencil and paper, and because together they contain almost every idea on the rest of the shelf. For each one you will see (1) what is done, (2) what a sensible classical person would predict, (3) what actually happens, with numbers, and (4) which classical idea has to go.
Experiment one: Stern–Gerlach magnets
The set-up

In 1922 Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach heated silver in an oven, let the atoms that escaped through a small hole fly as a narrow beam, and sent the beam between the poles of a specially shaped magnet. Each silver atom behaves like a tiny bar magnet (the magnetism comes from one unpaired electron). A uniform magnetic field would only twist such a bar magnet, but Stern and Gerlach shaped the poles so the field was stronger near one pole than the other. In a non-uniform field a tiny magnet feels a force, up or down, whose size depends on how its magnetic axis is tilted relative to the field direction. After the magnet, the atoms landed on a glass plate and left a mark.
What a classical physicist expects

Atoms come out of a hot oven with their tiny magnets pointing every which way. An atom whose magnet points straight up gets the biggest upward push, one pointing straight down gets the biggest downward push, and one lying sideways gets no push. Every tilt in between is possible, so the classical prediction is a continuous smear on the plate: a vertical stripe, densest in the middle.
What happens

The plate shows two separate spots, one above and one below, and nothing in between. Every atom is deflected by the same amount, either up or down. Half go each way. Let us call the magnet, which is oriented along the vertical $z$ direction, a Z magnet, and call the two results up and down.

This is already strange: the magnet seems to force every atom to answer a yes/no question, as if the tilt of the atom's magnet could only take two values. But it gets stranger when you put magnets in a row. Block the down beam, so only up atoms continue, and do the following.

items: Send the up atoms into a second Z magnet. Result: all of them come out up. None come out down. So the first magnet really did sort the atoms; whatever 'up' is, the atom keeps it.

Instead, turn the second magnet on its side, so it measures along the horizontal $x$ direction (an X magnet). Its two outputs are called $+x$ and $-x$. Result: half the up atoms go $+x$ and half go $-x$. That is not surprising yet: an atom pointing up has no reason to prefer left or right.

Now the key step. Keep only the $+x$ atoms from the X magnet and send them into a third magnet, a Z magnet again. These atoms were all selected as up by the first magnet. Result: half come out up and half come out down.

blocks.alt: Three magnets in a row. 1000 atoms enter a Z magnet; 500 go up and continue, 500 go down and are blocked. The 500 enter an X magnet; 250 go +x and continue. These 250 enter a second Z magnet and split 125 up, 125 down.
blocks.caption: The Z–X–Z experiment with ideal numbers. Without the middle magnet the last Z magnet would give 500 up and 0 down.

blocks.text: Working the numbers
Follow 1000 atoms through the Z–X–Z sequence, using the observed rule that a magnet at a right angle to the last one splits a beam evenly.

items: Step 1. The oven sends 1000 atoms into the first Z magnet. Half go up: 500 continue, 500 are blocked.
Step 2. The 500 up atoms enter the X magnet. Half go $+x$: 250 continue, 250 are blocked.
Step 3. The 250 $+x$ atoms enter the last Z magnet. Half go up and half go down: 125 and 125.

blocks.text: The simulation at the bottom of this page draws random outcomes with these probabilities; one run gave 491 up at the first magnet, 246 $+x$ at the second, and 126 up and 120 down at the last. When $N$ atoms are split at random half and half, the counts scatter around $N/2$ by roughly $\tfrac12\sqrt{N}$: for the 246 atoms at the last magnet that is $\tfrac12\sqrt{246} \approx 8$, so 126/120 is an ordinary run. Because the scatter grows only like $\sqrt{N}$ while the counts grow like $N$, the fractions get ever closer to one half as the number of atoms grows.
Which classical idea breaks

The natural classical explanation is that each atom carries two hidden labels, one saying up or down and one saying $+x$ or $-x$, and each magnet just reads its label. The first magnet keeps atoms labelled up; the second keeps atoms labelled $+x$; so the atoms entering the third magnet are all labelled up and $+x$, and the third magnet, reading the up/down label, should send all of them up. It sends half of them down.

So measuring along $x$ destroyed the result of measuring along $z$. The atoms do not carry a fixed answer to every question at once. Asking one question (X) changes the answer to another (Z). This is the first big idea: measurement changes the state of the thing measured, and some pairs of questions cannot both have definite answers at the same time. On the shelf this becomes the collapse rule on Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement) and non-commuting observables on Commutators and Compatible Observables (#/quantum/foundations/commutators).
Tilted magnets: the first quantitative rule
If the second magnet is tilted by an angle $\theta$ from the first instead of by $90^\circ$, the fraction of up atoms that come out on the 'up' side of the tilted magnet is

blocks.caption: Measured fraction for a spin-1/2 atom prepared up along z and measured along an axis tilted by θ.

blocks.text: Check the cases you already know. At $\theta = 0$ the magnets agree: $\cos^2 0 = 1$, everything goes up. At $\theta = 90^\circ$: $\cos^2 45^\circ = 0.5$, the even split. At $\theta = 180^\circ$ the second magnet is upside down, so the old 'up' is its 'down': $\cos^2 90^\circ = 0$. At $\theta = 60^\circ$: $\cos^2 30^\circ = 0.75$. Notice the angle is halved. 'Up' and 'down' point in opposite directions in space ($180^\circ$ apart) yet behave as completely distinct, perpendicular states in the mathematics ($90^\circ$ apart). That factor of two will reappear on the Bloch sphere, where a state at polar angle $\theta$ has amplitudes $\cos(\theta/2)$ and $\sin(\theta/2)$: The Qubit and the Bloch Sphere (#/quantum/qubits/bloch-sphere).

blocks.title: Check yourself: a tilted magnet
blocks.text: 1000 atoms, all up along $z$, enter a magnet tilted by $60^\circ$. The atoms that come out on its 'up' side then enter an ordinary Z magnet. About how many come out up at the end?
blocks.hint: After the first magnet the atoms are 'up along the tilted axis'. What angle separates that axis from $z$?
solution: Step 1. Tilted magnet: $P = \cos^2(60^\circ/2) = \cos^2 30^\circ = 0.75$, so about 750 atoms pass.
Step 2. These atoms are now 'up along the tilted axis'. The Z magnet is tilted by $60^\circ$ relative to that axis, so again $P(\text{up}) = 0.75$.
Step 3. $750 \times 0.75 = 562.5$, about 563 up, and $750 \times 0.25 = 187.5$, about 188 down.

blocks.text: Experiment two: three polarisers
The set-up

A polariser is a filter (the material in polarising sunglasses) with a preferred direction drawn across it. Light is a wave of electric field that wiggles in some direction across the beam; that direction is the polarisation. Ordinary light from a lamp is unpolarised: its wiggle direction changes randomly. A polariser lets through only the part of the wave wiggling along its preferred direction.
The classical wave rule, known since Étienne-Louis Malus in 1809, says: if light polarised at angle $0$ meets a polariser at angle $\theta$, the fraction of the intensity that gets through is

blocks.caption: Malus's law. Unpolarised light loses half its intensity at the first polariser, whatever its angle.

blocks.text: The paradox

Take two polarisers, one at $0^\circ$ and one at $90^\circ$ (crossed). Shine a lamp through them. Step 1: the first passes half the light, now polarised at $0^\circ$. Step 2: the second passes $\cos^2 90^\circ = 0$ of that. Nothing gets through; the pair looks black.
Now slide a third polariser, at $45^\circ$, between the two. You have added a filter, which can only remove light. Yet light now comes through. Work it out:

items: Step 1. First polariser ($0^\circ$): passes $\tfrac12$ of the unpolarised light.

Step 2. Middle polariser ($45^\circ$, a $45^\circ$ change): passes $\cos^2 45^\circ = \tfrac12$ of what arrives. Running total $\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. The light leaving it is polarised at $45^\circ$.
Step 3. Last polariser ($90^\circ$, again a $45^\circ$ change): passes $\tfrac12$ again. Total $\tfrac18 = 12.5\%$.

blocks.text: The middle filter does not just filter; it re-prepares the light at its own angle, and that new polarisation is no longer perpendicular to the last filter. It is the Z–X–Z story again: the middle measurement erases the result of the first. With more filters in between, each turning the polarisation by a smaller step, even more light gets through: with 2 extra filters (steps of $30^\circ$) the total is $\tfrac12(\cos^2 30^\circ)^3 = 0.211$, with 5 extra (steps of $15^\circ$) it is 0.330, with 50 extra it is 0.476, creeping up towards the $\tfrac12$ that a perfect, continuous rotation would give.
Why this is a quantum experiment

So far, waves explain everything: Malus's law is classical. The quantum part appears when you dim the lamp until light arrives one photon at a time. A photon cannot be split: a detector behind the filters either clicks or it does not. So what does 'one eighth of the light gets through' mean for a single photon? The only consistent answer is a probability. Each photon gets through all three filters with probability $\tfrac18$, independently of the others. In the simulation below, 12 536 of 100 000 single photons got through the $0^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $90^\circ$ stack, close to the expected 12 500.

This gives the second big idea: the theory does not say what one photon will do, only the probability of each outcome. And the probabilities come out as squares of cosines, $\cos^2\theta$, not as the cosines themselves. On the shelf, the cosine is an amplitude and its square is a probability; the rule is the Born rule on Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement).

blocks.title: Check yourself: where to put the middle filter
blocks.text: Crossed polarisers at $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$ have a third one between them at angle $\alpha$. What fraction of unpolarised light gets through for $\alpha = 30^\circ$, and which $\alpha$ lets through the most?
solution: Step 1. The fraction is $\tfrac12\cos^2\alpha\,\cos^2(90^\circ - \alpha)$.
Step 2. For $\alpha = 30^\circ$: $\tfrac12 \times 0.75 \times 0.25 = 0.09375$.

Step 3. $\cos\alpha\cos(90^\circ-\alpha) = \cos\alpha\sin\alpha = \tfrac12\sin 2\alpha$, so the fraction is $\tfrac18\sin^2 2\alpha$, largest when $2\alpha = 90^\circ$, that is $\alpha = 45^\circ$, giving $\tfrac18$.

blocks.text: Experiment three: one particle, two paths
The interferometer

The cleanest version of the famous double-slit experiment is the Mach–Zehnder interferometer. A photon meets a beam splitter, a half-silvered mirror that transmits half the light and reflects half. Two ordinary mirrors steer the two beams, along an upper path and a lower path, back together at a second beam splitter, which mixes them again and sends light to two detectors, D1 and D2. The two paths are made exactly the same length.

blocks.alt: A Mach-Zehnder interferometer: light from a source hits beam splitter 1, splits into an upper and a lower path, the paths are reflected by mirrors and recombined at beam splitter 2, which feeds detectors D1 and D2.
blocks.caption: Both paths open: every photon goes to D1. Block either path: half the photons are absorbed and the rest split evenly between D1 and D2.

blocks.text: The classical (probability) prediction

Send single photons in, one at a time. At the first beam splitter a photon goes up or down with probability $\tfrac12$ each. At the second, whichever path it took, it goes to D1 or D2 with probability $\tfrac12$ each. Adding up the ways: $P(\text{D1}) = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 + \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac12$, and the same for D2. Prediction: each detector clicks for half the photons.
What happens

Every photon arrives at D1. D2 never clicks. (Which detector gets everything depends on the exact path lengths and on how the splitters are made; with equal paths and the convention used here it is D1.) Now block the lower path with a piece of card. Half the photons are absorbed by the card. The other half, which took the upper path, now split evenly: a quarter of all photons go to D1 and a quarter to D2. Blocking a path, which only removes photons, has made D2 click where it never did before.
Amplitudes: the rule that works

Here is the rule that reproduces the experiment. Give every way something can happen a number called an amplitude. Along a path, multiply the amplitudes of the steps. If several paths lead to the same result and nothing records which path was taken, add their amplitudes. Only at the very end square the total to get a probability. For a beam splitter take the amplitudes $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ for each output, except one: light coming from the lower path and leaving towards D2 gets $-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$. (The minus sign is real physics: one of the reflections shifts the wave by half a cycle.) Then:

items: Step 1. To D1 via the upper path: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = \tfrac12$. Via the lower path: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = \tfrac12$. Total amplitude $\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1$. Probability $1^2 = 1$.

Step 2. To D2 via the upper path: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = \tfrac12$. Via the lower path: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\left(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right) = -\tfrac12$. Total $\tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0$. Probability $0$.

Step 3. Lower path blocked: only the upper path remains. To D1: amplitude $\tfrac12$, probability $\tfrac14$. To D2: amplitude $\tfrac12$, probability $\tfrac14$. The other $\tfrac12$ is absorbed by the card. This matches the experiment exactly.

blocks.text: The probability rule failed because probabilities are never negative, so they can only pile up. Amplitudes can be negative, so two ways of reaching D2 can cancel. This cancelling is called destructive interference; the piling up at D1 is constructive interference. Interference needs the paths to be indistinguishable: blocking one path (or even just recording which path the photon took) removes the cancelling.
Adding a phase

Lengthen the lower path very slightly with a sheet of glass. The light on that path then arrives a fraction of a wave late. In the amplitude rule this multiplies the lower path's amplitude by a phase factor, a complex number $e^{i\varphi}$ of size 1 (Complex Numbers for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/complex-numbers) explains these). The amplitude to reach D1 becomes $\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 e^{i\varphi}$, and its squared size works out to $P(\text{D1}) = \cos^2(\varphi/2)$. (The few lines of algebra need the rules for complex numbers; they are done in the section on adding amplitudes on Complex Numbers for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/complex-numbers).) At $\varphi = 0$ the phase factor is 1, the amplitude is $\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1$ and $P(\text{D1}) = 1$; at $\varphi = 90^\circ$, $P(\text{D1}) = \cos^2 45^\circ = 0.5$; at $\varphi = 180^\circ$ the phase factor is $-1$, the amplitude is $\tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0$, and every photon now goes to D2. Sliding the glass in smoothly sweeps the photons back and forth between the detectors. That is why amplitudes must be complex numbers: a delay is a turn of the phase, and only complex numbers turn.
The double slit, one dot at a time

The double-slit experiment is the same physics with many paths. Particles (photons, electrons, even large molecules) pass through two narrow slits and land on a screen. With one slit open they make a single smooth blob. With both open they make a pattern of bright and dark stripes (fringes): at a dark stripe the amplitudes from the two slits cancel, so fewer particles land there than with one slit open. In 1989 Akira Tonomura's group at Hitachi sent electrons through an electron version of the experiment so slowly that only one was ever in the apparatus. Each electron made one dot at a random place. After a few dozen dots the pattern looked random; after thousands the stripes were plain.

The simulation below does this with dots drawn from the two-slit probability pattern. Counting dots in nine strips across the screen (centred on bright, dark, bright, ... positions) gives, for 10 dots, 1 1 2 1 4 0 1 0 0: no visible pattern. For 100 dots: 11 3 25 4 24 7 18 2 6; the alternation is showing. For 10 000 dots: 1006 339 2021 508 2409 487 1957 329 944, unmistakable fringes. Adding the patterns of each slit open on its own (the probability rule) gives 628 958 1245 1373 1459 1505 1268 940 624: a smooth hump with no stripes.
For a single point on the screen, if slit 1 alone gives probability $P_1$ and slit 2 alone gives $P_2$, the probability rule says $P_1 + P_2$; the amplitude rule says

blocks.caption: φ is the phase difference between the two amplitudes at that point on the screen.

blocks.text: The last term, the interference term, is what the probability rule leaves out. With $P_1 = P_2 = 0.1$ the result can be anything from $0$ (at $\varphi = 180^\circ$) to $0.4$ (at $\varphi = 0$); the classical value 0.2 appears only where $\cos\varphi = 0$.

blocks.title: Check yourself: detecting a block without touching it
blocks.text: In the balanced interferometer (all photons to D1 when both paths are open), you are told the lower path may or may not be blocked. You send one photon and D2 clicks. What do you now know, and in what fraction of trials with the path blocked does this happen?
blocks.hint: Compare $P(\text{D2})$ with and without the block.
solution: Step 1. With both paths open, D2 has probability 0, so a D2 click is impossible if nothing blocks the lower path.
Step 2. So a D2 click proves the block is there, even though the photon that clicked took the upper path and never touched it.
Step 3. With the block in place, the probabilities are $\tfrac12$ absorbed, $\tfrac14$ D1, $\tfrac14$ D2. So one trial in four gives this proof.
blocks.answer: The path is certainly blocked; this happens in 1/4 of trials with the block in place.

blocks.text: This is the Elitzur–Vaidman 'bomb tester' (1993), a striking way to see that the unused path matters: whether it is open changes where a photon that did not take it can go.
What a theory has to supply
Put the three experiments side by side and a list of requirements appears. Any theory of these experiments must have:

items: States described by amplitudes. A photon in the interferometer is described by an amplitude for each path, and amplitudes add and cancel. Because a delay turns the phase, amplitudes are complex numbers. A list of complex amplitudes is a vector, so states are vectors: Linear Algebra for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/linear-algebra) and States and Dirac Notation (#/quantum/foundations/states-and-dirac-notation).

Probabilities as squared sizes of amplitudes. Single events are random; the theory gives probabilities $\vert\text{amplitude}\vert^2$, which is why $\cos^2$ keeps appearing: Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement).

Measurement that changes the state. After a Z magnet, the atom is 'up' and stays up; after an X magnet, its up-ness is gone. A measurement leaves the system in a state that matches its outcome: Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement).

Questions that do not have answers at the same time. Z and X cannot both be definite. In the mathematics this is two matrices whose product depends on the order: Commutators and Compatible Observables (#/quantum/foundations/commutators) and Observables and Uncertainty (#/quantum/foundations/observables-and-uncertainty).

Smooth change between measurements. The glass slab turns a phase continuously; between measurements the state evolves smoothly and reversibly: The Schrödinger Equation (#/quantum/dynamics/schrodinger-equation).

blocks.text: There is one more experiment, not on this page, that cannot be explained even by giving each particle secret instructions in advance: measurements on two separated, entangled particles (Bell inequalities). It needs the tools of the whole Foundations and Qubits chapters; the Many-Body chapter builds up to it, starting from Composite Systems and Tensor Products (#/quantum/many-body/composite-systems) and Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement), and a later page treats it in full.
Putting it together

blocks.title: A Stern–Gerlach puzzle in full
blocks.text: 1000 atoms from the oven go through: a Z magnet (keep up), an X magnet (keep $+x$), an X magnet again (keep $+x$), and finally a Z magnet. How many come out of each port of the last magnet? Then remove the middle two magnets and say how many come out up and down at a Z magnet placed straight after the first.
blocks.hint: Treat each magnet in turn: the atoms entering it are in the state the previous kept magnet selected.
solution: Step 1. First Z magnet: 500 up continue.
Step 2. First X magnet: these are up atoms at $90^\circ$ to $x$, so $\cos^2 45^\circ = \tfrac12$: 250 go $+x$.
Step 3. Second X magnet: the atoms are already $+x$ and the magnet agrees ($\theta = 0$): all 250 go $+x$ again. Repeating a measurement gives the same answer.
Step 4. Last Z magnet: $+x$ atoms at $90^\circ$ to $z$: half up, half down, 125 and 125.
Step 5. Without the X magnets, the 500 up atoms meet a Z magnet that agrees with the first: all 500 up, none down.
blocks.answer: 125 up and 125 down; without the X magnets, 500 up and 0 down

blocks.text: Key points

items: Stern–Gerlach: a measurement gives one of a few discrete results, and measuring along $x$ erases what was known about $z$.
A spin prepared along one axis and measured along an axis tilted by $\theta$ gives 'up' with probability $\cos^2(\theta/2)$.
Three polarisers: inserting a filter can let more light through, because a measurement re-prepares the state. For single photons the fractions are probabilities.
Interferometers and double slits: probabilities do not add; amplitudes do, and amplitudes can cancel. Probability is the squared size of the total amplitude.
Interference needs indistinguishable paths; blocking or recording the path destroys it.
Path delays turn phases, so amplitudes are complex numbers.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Four polarisers
blocks.text: Polarisers at $0^\circ$, $30^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$ are stacked in that order. What fraction of unpolarised light gets through? What is the probability that one photon gets through?
blocks.hint: Each step multiplies by $\cos^2$ of the change in angle.
solution: Step 1. First polariser: $\tfrac12$.
Step 2. Three further steps of $30^\circ$, each passing $\cos^2 30^\circ = 0.75$.
Step 3. $\tfrac12 \times 0.75^3 = \tfrac12 \times 0.421875 = 0.2109$. For one photon this fraction is the probability.

blocks.title: Many small steps
blocks.text: Between crossed polarisers you insert $n$ extra polarisers, equally spaced. Write the fraction that gets through, and evaluate it for $n = 5$.
solution: Step 1. There are $n+1$ steps from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$, each of $90^\circ/(n+1)$.
Step 2. Fraction $= \tfrac12\left[\cos^2\left(\frac{90^\circ}{n+1}\right)\right]^{n+1}$.
Step 3. For $n = 5$: steps of $15^\circ$, $\cos^2 15^\circ = 0.9330$, and $0.9330^6 = 0.6597$, so the fraction is $0.330$.

blocks.title: Interferometer with a phase
blocks.text: In the balanced interferometer, a glass plate in the lower path adds a phase $\varphi = 60^\circ$. Using $P(\text{D1}) = \cos^2(\varphi/2)$, what fraction of 10 000 photons reach each detector? What phase sends equal numbers to both?
solution: Step 1. $P(\text{D1}) = \cos^2 30^\circ = 0.75$, so about 7500 photons go to D1 and 2500 to D2.
Step 2. Equal numbers need $\cos^2(\varphi/2) = \tfrac12$, so $\varphi/2 = 45^\circ$, $\varphi = 90^\circ$.
blocks.answer: about 7500 to D1 and 2500 to D2; φ = 90°

blocks.title: Two slits at one point
blocks.text: At a point on a double-slit screen, slit 1 alone gives probability $0.04$ and slit 2 alone gives $0.09$ (per unit of screen). What are the smallest and largest probabilities with both open, and what does the probability rule predict?
solution: Step 1. Probability rule: $0.04 + 0.09 = 0.13$.
Step 2. The interference term is $2\sqrt{0.04\times0.09}\cos\varphi = 2\times0.06\cos\varphi = 0.12\cos\varphi$.
Step 3. Largest at $\cos\varphi = 1$: $0.13 + 0.12 = 0.25$. Smallest at $\cos\varphi = -1$: $0.13 - 0.12 = 0.01$.
blocks.answer: between 0.01 and 0.25; the probability rule says 0.13

blocks.text: Simulating the three experiments

The code draws random outcomes with the rules from this page: $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ for tilted magnets, Malus's law for polarisers, amplitudes for the interferometer (the beam splitter modelled as the matrix that sends $(1, 0)$ to $(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})$ and $(0, 1)$ to $(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})$), and dots sampled from a two-slit pattern. Running it reproduces every number quoted above.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)

# 1. Stern-Gerlach: a spin prepared "up along z" meets a magnet tilted by angle theta.
#    Quantum rule: P(up along the new axis) = cos^2(theta/2).
def sg(theta_deg, n_atoms):
    p_up = np.cos(np.radians(theta_deg) / 2) ** 2
    return int((rng.random(n_atoms) < p_up).sum())
print("Stern-Gerlach, 1000 atoms already 'up along z' meeting a tilted magnet:")
for th in (0, 60, 90, 120, 180):
    print(f"  tilt {th:3d} deg: rule says {np.cos(np.radians(th)/2)**2:.3f}, simulated up count {sg(th, 1000)}")

# Z, then X, then Z on 1000 atoms from the oven (each magnet: keep the 'up'/'+' beam only for the first two)
n = 1000
up1 = sg(90, n)        # oven atoms are random: 50/50 at the first magnet (same numbers as tilt 90)
plus = sg(90, up1)     # z-up atoms into an X magnet (tilt 90 deg)
up3 = sg(90, plus)     # x-plus atoms into a Z magnet
print(f"Z-X-Z: {n} in, {up1} up at magnet 1, {plus} '+x' at magnet 2, {up3} up / {plus-up3} down at magnet 3")

# 2. Polarisers: Malus's law, transmitted fraction cos^2(angle between successive polarisers)
def chain(angles_deg):
    frac = 0.5                                  # unpolarised light: the first polariser passes half
    for a, b in zip(angles_deg[:-1], angles_deg[1:]):
        frac *= np.cos(np.radians(b - a)) ** 2
    return frac
print("Polarisers (fraction of unpolarised light that gets through):")
print("  0, 90        :", round(chain([0, 90]), 4))
print("  0, 45, 90    :", round(chain([0, 45, 90]), 4))
for k in (3, 6, 11, 51):
    print(f"  {k-1:2d} extra in between (steps of {90/k:.2f} deg):", round(chain(list(np.linspace(0, 90, k + 1))), 4))
photons = 100000
passed = (rng.random(photons) < chain([0, 45, 90])).sum()
print(f"  single photons through 0,45,90: {passed} of {photons} got through")

# 3. Mach-Zehnder: amplitudes add, then square. Beam splitter modelled as the Hadamard (1/sqrt2)[[1,1],[1,-1]].
BS = np.array([[1, 1], [1, -1]]) / np.sqrt(2)
def mz(phi, block=None):
    a = BS @ np.array([1, 0], complex)          # after splitter 1: amplitudes for (upper, lower)
    a[1] *= np.exp(1j * phi)                    # extra phase on the lower path
    lost = 0.0
    if block is not None:
        lost = abs(a[block]) ** 2; a[block] = 0 # a block absorbs that path's amplitude
    out = BS @ a                                # splitter 2: amplitudes for (D1, D2)
    return abs(out[0]) ** 2, abs(out[1]) ** 2, lost
print("Mach-Zehnder probabilities (D1, D2, absorbed):")
for phi in (0, np.pi / 2, np.pi):
    print(f"  phase {phi:.3f}: ", tuple(round(float(x), 3) for x in mz(phi)))
print("  lower path blocked:", tuple(round(float(x), 3) for x in mz(0, block=1)))

# 4. Double slit, one dot at a time: intensity ~ cos^2(pi d x / (lambda L)) * sinc^2(pi a x / (lambda L))
x = np.linspace(-1.125, 1.125, 2251)            # screen position (arbitrary units); bright fringes at 0, +-0.5, +-1
I_both = np.cos(2 * np.pi * x) ** 2 * np.sinc(x / 2) ** 2
I_sum = 0.5 * np.sinc(x / 2) ** 2               # one slit at a time, added: |a1|^2 + |a2|^2, same envelope, no fringes
print("Double slit, dots counted in 9 strips centred at -1, -0.75, ..., +1 (bright fringes at -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1):")
for N in (10, 100, 10000):
    dots = rng.choice(x, size=N, p=I_both / I_both.sum())
    h, _ = np.histogram(dots, bins=9, range=(-1.125, 1.125))
    print(f"  {N:5d} dots, counts:", " ".join(f"{c}" for c in h))
dots = rng.choice(x, size=10000, p=I_sum / I_sum.sum())
h, _ = np.histogram(dots, bins=9, range=(-1.125, 1.125))
print("  10000 dots, one slit open at a time (added):", " ".join(f"{c}" for c in h))

blocks.text: Where this is used

items: Every rule this page found by experiment is stated precisely, in the language of vectors, on the Foundations pages, starting with Complex Numbers for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/complex-numbers).
The interferometer is the simplest quantum circuit: Hadamard, phase, Hadamard. It is worked through as a qubit on Interference of Amplitudes (#/quantum/qubits/interference).

In quantum reservoir computing, measurement erasing information (the Z–X–Z effect) is the root of the measurement back-action problem: Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action).
